author: Holly Jonas
title: How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want
content:
This article 

How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Kumi Naidoo knows a thing or two about activism. He has organized anti-apartheid school boycotts in South Africa, scaled oil rigs in frigid Arctic waters and called out world leaders for their moral failures in U.N. climate negotiations. But it was not until he eulogized a glacier that he truly realized the potent alchemy of arts, culture and activism — also known as artivism.




With decades of experience in social movements and serving in top leadership positions in international NGOs, Naidoo is better placed than most to shed light on the inner workings of activism. He is also refreshingly candid about its shortcomings. One of the biggest challenges in activism, he says, is a communications deficit. His late son, South African rapper and singer Riky Rick, lovingly pushed him to ditch the technical jargon so commonly used by climate activists and instead reach people through the heart, body and soul.




After the musician’s devastating and sudden passing in 2022, Riky’s mother Louisa, widow Bianca, and Kumi channeled their grief and resolve into the Riky Rick Foundation for the Promotion of Artivism. One of their key initiatives, 

Global Artivism

, highlights the power of arts and culture to contribute to positive change, helps cultural creatives connect and collaborate with each other, and surfaces and works to address the many challenges they face. Powered by a team of volunteers and a lean staff, in-person global convenings in South Africa and Brazil and regional virtual convenings have helped mobilize and further energize this vibrant movement. They are now in the thick of the decentralized 

Global Artivism Month

, which will culminate on International Human Rights Day on Dec. 10.




In this interview with Naidoo, who also serves as president of the 

Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative

, he discusses the power and potential of the global artivism movement, how pessimism is a luxury we cannot afford, and the continuing prescience of Martin Luther King Jr.




This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.




For those who may not be familiar with it, what is artivism, and what are the connections between artivism and nonviolent movements?




Artivism is the intersection of arts, culture and activism. Its intention is to address a major weakness in much of our activism, which is that we have aimed our messages and our narratives at the brain, and we’ve ignored the heart, the body and the soul. A song or documentary reaches many more people than a policy brief does. Politics does not drive culture; culture drives politics.




Harnessing the power of arts and culture on its own will not deliver salvation from the climate crisis and the intersecting crises that emerge from it. However, failing to harness the power of arts and culture almost guarantees that we’re going to fail because we’re never going to reach the large numbers of people that we need to.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










We are facing a massive global mental health crisis coming from ecological and climate anxiety, war, conflict, deepening inequality, authoritarianism and fascism. Artivism has the potential to invite people into the biggest struggles of our time, in a way that creates opportunities for participation and engagement. To help us secure peace, justice and all of the good things that we want, those in power have no incentive to actually listen to what we’re saying unless we can show we have a powerful constituency.




We also need this massive mobilization and participation because participation itself will be part of the antidote to despair, despondency and depression. We can be the best versions of ourselves in this current moment if we keep a positive disposition, despite how bad things are. In this moment of history, pessimism is a luxury we simply cannot afford. The pessimism that justifiably emerges from our analysis, our lived experiences and observations can and must be responded to with the optimism of our thought, our action, our creativity, our courage and our sense of humanity.




Joyful acts of cultural expression, in which hope is embedded, offer us the best way forward. Artivism is typically nonviolent, creative and speaks to the heart. I believe artivism has a big role in the quest to create a world where we value peace and we value nonviolence.




Could you tell us about your “origin story” as an activist and how you got involved in artivism?




As a young anti-apartheid activist in South Africa, we were organizing amongst people who had low levels of literacy and education. We used all sorts of arts and culture — sport, cooking, music. Even during the state of emergency, when we could not have meetings, we held rock concerts and called them things like “groove to improve.” They were soft messages, but everybody attending was going there to resist the apartheid regime. So artivism was always part of me.







Kumi Naidoo at the Second Global Artivism Convening in Salvador, Brazil, in November 2025. (Garimpo/Global Artivism Initiative)







But when I was the head of Greenpeace and Amnesty International, those roles were so bureaucratic in some ways that that side of me got subdued. At Greenpeace, we were talking about 1.5 degrees and 350 parts per million, which means nothing to at least 90 percent of people in the world. I started engaging more and more with the arts and culture community because I knew we needed their creativity to help us communicate in a more powerful way. Then I had an epiphany moment in August 2019, when the artist Olafur Eliasson invited me to go to Iceland to join a 

funeral for a glacier

.




Early in the morning, the former President of Ireland [and U.N. Human Rights Commissioner], Mary Robinson and I offered comments and about 500 of us walked up the Okjökull glacier. When we looked at the media coverage later, I would say it was more successful than 95 percent of the actions that happened during my leadership of Greenpeace. Instead of drowning people in an acronym alphabet soup, we talked about loss. We connected with a human emotion that people could easily understand.




On the flight from Reykjavik back to London, I decided to step down as the head of Amnesty. I could have potentially stayed several more years, but I really felt I needed to address this communications deficit of activism.




In September 2021, I went to Berlin to focus on artivism as a 

fellow

 of the Robert Bosch Academy, but I was soon back in South Africa. Archbishop Desmond Tutu passed away that December. After the funeral, our son [South African rapper and singer Riky Rick] sat his mom and me down and said, “You’re not really good at what you do. You’ve been fighting for democracy, human rights, gender equity and so on since you were teenagers. When I look at the world, it’s all moving in the wrong direction.” When I asked him why we are failing, he said, “It’s very simple. You aim all the narratives at the brain, and you ignore the heart, the body and the soul. … It sounds like you’re speaking a version of English that only one percent of people in the world understand. How are you going to move people?” He was just amazing at being able to speak to working-class and middle-class people.




A month later, he called me, and he was down. I cheered him up, and he said he was going to visit me in Berlin and bring his wife and mom. But then a week later, he died by suicide.




After his passing, we set up the 

Riky Rick Foundation for the Promotion of Artivism

. We started building a global network, which has now led into the global artivism movement.




I’m so sorry again for his passing, it must still be so painful. How would you describe the role of the Foundation in relation to the global artivism movement?




We are not creating something new, but energizing and amplifying what already exists. We see our role as very modest. We see the movement per se as much broader and living in virtually every community, where culture is alive and well in its multiple, diverse manifestations. What we hope to do is to amplify its power and encourage folks to not see culture as decoration, but to see culture as power.




What do you consider as “good practices” of the artivism movement in the current context? What still needs to evolve in terms of strategy and tactics to meet the moment?




One of the roles that cultural creatives have played historically, which is the most needed role right now, is to help us imagine futures and realities yet to be born. We need the cultural community to help us imagine a world where there’s greater equality, greater peace, greater justice, greater love, less division and less conflict across the artificial boundaries that opportunistic politicians are driving today.




Artivism also gives people a sense of hope and optimism and creates spaces of joy. People are so time-poor today, sometimes working two or three jobs to get by. If they have a little time to give, you’re most likely to get them to come to an event if it not only has a purpose and a good message behind it, but it is also fun.




Cultural action is going to be an asset to help people get through this moment. We should not underestimate the need for fun right now. Don’t let the Trumps of the world rob you of your right to joy and happiness. Sing, dance, be joyful! Even when things are bad, smile at your oppressor.




I would like to hear your thoughts on the critiques and limitations of artivism. Some people say the arts are just a “nice to have.” There are also concerns about the art world being a space of privilege, with limited access for folks in working-class communities. How do you respond to those critiques?




Those are really important observations. The global artivism movement embraces cultural action for a safe and just world. Harnessing the power of arts and culture alone does not deliver salvation, so let’s not overstate it. But let’s also recognize the world of arts and culture is very broad and diverse, with everything from cuisine and fashion to music and visual art.




Some of the very high-end practices are highly problematic, such as fossil fuel companies buying off and branding museums, which already carry a lot of pain for the 88 percent of people who come from the Global South.




Artists and activists create paintings using ashes gathered from previous forest fires, during at the Second Global Artivism Convening in Salvador, Brazil, in November 2025. (Garimpo/Global Artivism Initiative)




The global artivism movement is mostly concerned about frontline artists who are rooted in communities, who are living the pain, who are not already established. While that’s our focus, we are engaging with everybody and trying to keep a broad tent approach.




We’re also saying to the artists who have made it, “You know how hard it was to get there.” We also have to be careful about it not being extractive. Global South culture has always been extracted by the North in multiple ways, and the arts world is not without contradiction and challenge. … We hope more resources flow to community arts efforts.




One of the most amazing things about Riky was that he quietly helped a lot of people as a philanthropist. He directly supported more than 100 individual artists in multiple ways, without a foundation or tax breaks. We only realized this after he died. He was a superstar in South Africa, but once he made it, he didn’t think, “Oh, it’s all about me now. How do I keep accumulating?”




What is the role of artivism in the context of closing or closed civic space and authoritarian regimes?




The shrinking of civic space has also led to thousands of artists around the world being at risk. The organization Artists at Risk is documenting the challenges that Sudanese, Palestinian, Ukrainian, Russian and other artists are facing in horrendous civic space realities. It’s also an indicator that artists have unique power in this current moment.




Artivism can open up avenues of creative public participation and pressure that can sometimes beat the restrictions of repressive authoritarian governments. It offers not only hope, but also the space to imagine realities in the future that could be much better and much different from the unjust realities of the present.




Grassroots artists may face financial precarity, and maybe even family or societal ostracization, in addition to threats they may face for being activists. How can social movements better support artivists and contribute to their individual and collective protection and well-being?




For far too long, the image of an activist was somebody who worked excessive hours and took excessive risks. We have to change the image of what an activist is. Of course, people who occupy oil rigs and lead marches are a very important part of the broader activist community. However, we have been very negligent about not sufficiently recognizing the massive trauma that human rights and environmental activists experience.




We are dealing with a global mental health crisis right now. Sometimes the pressure to just keep going means that we are not creating enough circles of support around activists who are experiencing primary and secondary trauma through the communities they’re working with and the injustice and suffering they are witnessing. We must not underestimate this.




For people who are putting their lives on the line to work for a more just future, it’s okay to take a break every now and then. Not only is it okay, it’s critically important that you build circles of support around you.




For the level of popular mobilization we need, whether it’s painting murals, running soup kitchens, building micro solar grids or protesting, all of these forms of participation are going to be necessary to pressure those with political and economic power to act with the urgency that the situation calls for.




What advice or guidance could you share with civil society and movement leaders who would like to engage more in artivism, but are unsure of how to start or sustain it?




One of the biggest challenges that activism faces historically and at the moment is that we face a massive communications deficit. We are not able to communicate to the large numbers of people that we absolutely need to reach. In fact, those who are promoting fascism and authoritarianism have found more effective ways to weaponize identity and culture to misinform and to get people to vote for the most awful racist, sexist, war-mongering regimes in the world.




There is an objective challenge: The people who own the powerful media communication channels are vested in the status quo, whether it’s the military-industrial complex or the fossil fuel-industrial complex. They are not inclined to give equitable coverage to ideas that contest that status quo, such as our dependency on fossil fuels.




For civil society organizations wanting to communicate more effectively and reach out to the artists and cultural creatives in your communities, engage them with respect, embrace the power of culture as a central part of shifting the needle and moving more people to embrace the need for urgent action. We are losing valuable time with the climate emergency getting worse and worse by the day.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Artists are not waiting for mainstream civil society organizations to come and educate them. Many artists are already doing amazing work, based on their own understanding of the realities in their communities and in the world. Some have better ideas than formal civil society organizations on how to communicate more effectively. There needs to be a multifaceted approach, and the bottom line is embracing the power of arts and culture for a safe and just world.




You have spoken before about creative maladjustment, drawing inspiration from Martin Luther King’s popularization of this term in the 1960s. What does this mean to you in the current moment, with so many intersecting crises?




Soon after I was born, King gave a 

speech

 in which he talked about the term “maladjusted” from the field of psychology.




“[W]e all want to live the well-adjusted life in order to avoid neurotic and schizophrenic personalities. But,” he said, “there are some things in our nation and some things in the world [to] which I am proud to be maladjusted.”




He continued, “I never intend to adjust myself to segregation and discrimination. I never intend to adjust myself to religious bigotry. I never intend to become adjusted to economic conditions which will take necessities from the many to give luxuries to the few. I never intend to adjust to the madness of militarism and the self-defeating effects of physical violence.”




If this wisdom was true in 1965, it is a thousand times more relevant now in the United States as well as virtually every country around the world. Today, his logic is informing thousands of activists and multiple movements as we push back against the status quo that is broken, unjust and driving humanity to war, climate disaster and many other challenges. If there was a moment in human history in which the idea of creative maladjustment is needed more than ever, I would argue that moment is now.

How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want

title: Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships
content:
This article 

Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







What comes next for American democracy? Our research into authoritarian regimes reveals a striking pattern in how autocracies begin to fall apart — and democracy starts to regain ground.




The 2026 U.S. midterms revealed deep and growing frustration with the Trump administration, including among communities that 

have traditionally

 supported Republicans. The secretary of the army, a Trump appointee, 

resigned

 after disputes over military readiness and the Iran war. Small businesses 

sued

 the administration over tariffs, while companies denounced ICE raids for gutting profits. The CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, a three-time Trump voter, 

attacked the administration

 over ICE raids, saying that “South Texas will never be red again.” On Nov. 3, his prediction came true as Texas border counties 

saw historic swings

 toward the Democratic party. These signs reveal widening cracks in alliances that have kept Trump in power.




This expanding circle of dissent evokes a common global pattern: When compliance with an authoritarian leader begins to break down, it can trigger a cascade of opposition that ultimately leads to regime collapse. Brazilian businesses that backed Jair Bolsonaro eventually denounced his anti-democratic behaviors, contributing to his electoral defeat. When parts of the Catholic Church removed support from the far-right Law and Justice Party in Poland, its governing coalition fragmented. And in Hungary, the electoral coalition that brought down Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was led by defectors from Orbán’s own party.  




When and why do people stop complying with dictators? We studied the behavior of thousands of key social groups whose compliance is critical for dictatorships to remain in power. These include businesses, unions, security forces and faith groups, key pillars whose political, economic and moral resources keep regimes standing. Looking at dictatorships and backsliding democracies in the post-Cold War era, one clear pattern stands out: Broad civic mobilization 

and

 dense social ties between those complying with the regime and members of a pro-democracy opposition encourages non-compliance. Mass noncompliance is how autocracies fall. Indeed, the 

chances of stopping democratic backsliding

 while relying only on institutional channels like litigation, legislation and voting is about 7.5 percent. The presence of a broad-based civil resistance increases the probability of success to around 53 percent.  










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Both broad mobilization and social connection are crucial because of the nature of compliance. While some people comply because of true ideological alignment, most do so for more ordinary reasons: to advance careers, protect business interests, show deference to authority, or out of simple psychological inertia. Others may for their safety. When people fear political retaliation, public support can mask private indifference or even opposition. For example, while farm bureaus across the U.S. may avoid publicly denouncing the administration, plenty of farmers and ranchers are 

seething

. While big business has largely refrained from publicly criticizing the administration, 

behind closed doors

 many CEOs are exasperated. A pro-democracy front should make room for people withdrawing their support for all of these reasons.  




Broad-based civic mobilization — where diverse groups use 

protests

, marches, 

boycotts

 and walkouts to push back — changes this picture. If people both see and believe that dissent is widespread, they are more likely to shift their behavior. Courage becomes contagious. 




Strong social ties between a regime’s pillars of support and its opponents can facilitate a cascade of dissent. If people only see those who are different from them protesting, their dissent is easy to dismiss as the actions of a radical few. Yet if those they know and trust begin to speak out, such actions are more difficult to discount. This helps explain why the 

spread of protests

 into rural and traditionally conservative parts of the U.S. is noteworthy. In Tunisia’s “Jasmine Revolution,” the national labor union — initially a co-opted part of the Ben Ali dictatorship — shifted to supporting the revolution when local offices that had been regularly hosting protest meetings demanded national action. In Minnesota, close relationships between communities facing violent immigration enforcement and businesses, religious groups and unions led to the mass mobilization that ended Operation Metro Surge.




Dialogue with members of regime-supporting pillars can encourage them to stop complying. For example, in Serbia in 2000, student activists and opposition political party leaders organizing against President Slobodan Milosevic held 10 days of quiet backroom meetings with police and military leaders in the lead up to a major day of protest, assuring them that Milosevic’s ouster would not threaten them. When the day of protest arrived, almost all police and military units stood aside. When the federal administration tried to compel nine U.S. universities to adopt anti-DEI policies or risk losing federal funding, strategic dialogue between student unions, businesses and university administrators, combined with pressure from students and alumni, prompted all of the schools to 

reject the compact

. 




Loyalty shifts are always difficult. Dense social ties and outreach alone may be insufficient to shift incentives for supporters. Pressure tactics, including consumer boycotts, strikes and economic shutdowns are often needed to raise the costs of complying with the status quo. The scale of mass mobilization in Minneapolis in response to Operation Metro Surge, particularly following the killings of two protesters, encouraged an unprecedented 

business statement

 calling for de-escalation. Fierce 

grassroots pressure

 prompted Citizens Bank to cut ties with two detention management companies it financed. The ICE Out of MN 

general strike

 led by unions, faith groups, immigrant rights organizations, small businesses, ordinary Minnesotans and people from across the country, who called for “No work, No school, No shopping” on Jan. 23, helped end the federal operation.    
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













For pro-democracy movements, two lessons are clear: First, public dissent can puncture the bubble of fear or indifference that keeps pillars of support compliant. Second, deepening ties with members of key pillars of regime support, particularly those suffering regime harms like political retribution, corruption and instability, can help move them into action. Outreach to disaffected farmers, veterans and business leaders can make a difference, particularly when they believe people they know and trust have their backs. Dialogue, combined with pressure, can help erode the pillars of support autocrats rely on until the edifice falls apart, making way for a pluralistic democracy. Understanding the strategies and tactics for moving members of key pillars, including the sequencing of engagement and pressure, is at the heart of the 

Common Courage pillars activation training

 that the Horizons Project has developed with partners. 




The midterms and recent defections from the Trump administration offer a powerful reminder that political loyalties are not fixed. They may also mark the beginning of a tipping point. Yet it is crucial to not read this moment as necessarily the beginning of the end. Overcoming autocrats is a process 

fraught with challenge

. History reveals that autocracies rarely fall apart all at once: one person or institution withdraws its support, then another, until isolated acts of dissent become something larger.  




The question for the next two years is whether the cracks we’re seeing will widen into that kind of cascade — and whether this electoral shift and broader moment of dissent can become something more enduring: a rebuilding of American democracy.

author: Mehran Khalili
title: What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?
content:
This article 

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







It was a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and several marches were converging on Syntagma Square in Athens, the epicenter of Greek protest. There were teachers on strike, university students who’d camped in the square overnight, and high schoolers holding painted banners that read “From Greece to France, we’re fighting for modern schools.” Parents pushed strollers through the growing crowd, their toddlers looking on in wonder.




But not everyone was there for the same reason. Groups of black-clad young men ducking in and out of the march, faces covered, were play-fighting each other in a way that looked like a rehearsal. Riot police were lining the side streets, watching over it all with the bored expression of men waiting for their shift to end. And photojournalists were circling, hoping for the youths and the police to meet in a burst of violence that would pay for their day.




The violence didn’t happen this time. According to the 

police count

, 10,000 people marched peacefully through central Athens. Afterwards, people hung around, arguing about politics and passing water bottles in the autumn sun. 




I keep thinking about those bored riot police, though, because they seemed to understand what organizers sometimes don’t: A government that has seen a lot of marches knows how to wait one out. The question for the teachers and students in Athens — and in Paris, Milan, Brussels, Lisbon, Madrid, Berlin, Vienna, Tirana and every other city caught up in Europe’s autumn of protest — is how to make saying no cost their governments more than saying yes.




An autumn of anger




The energy in Europe’s streets is bigger than many realize.  Young people have been protesting in at least nine European countries this autumn, most of them since mid-September. 




In France, a walkout over the lack of teachers at one high school in Créteil in September 

spread to hundreds of schools

 within weeks. By mid-October, about 550,000 people (by the 

government’s own count

) were marching in cities and towns across the country. In Spain and Portugal, the anger is about housing. Protesters set up camps in 

Madrid’s Puerta del Sol

 and 

Lisbon’s Rossio,

 and on Nov. 11, Spain’s tenants’ unions, backed by the big trade unions, held the country’s 

first general strike in 14 years.

 It came after Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old widow in fragile health, was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for most of her life. She 

died in hospital

 two weeks later.




Demonstrators march for the right to housing  after the eviction of  an 87-year-old woman from the home where she had lived for around seventy years in Madrid, Spain. (Wikimedia Commons)




The grievances overlap without being the same. It’s about schools in France and Greece, university tuition in 

Belgium

 and 

Albania

, university budgets in 

Austria

, military conscription in 

Germany

, and rent in Portugal and Spain, where the average rent is now 

98.7 percent

 of what a young person earns in a month. But running beneath most of them is a familiar story: governments that say there’s no money for schools, or for people who are struggling, always, somehow, manage to find it for something else, often weapons.




In France, Germany and 

Italy

, protesters have made that link. France’s 

2027 budget

 adds $7 billion for defense and just $1.2 billion for schools, while 

cutting 1,588 teaching posts

. In Germany, young people marched in more than 30 cities on Oct. 31, angry, as 

Al Jazeera reported

, that military spending is rising while education funding is cut. 




The protests have achieved some modest wins. On Oct. 26, France’s government promised to 

replace Parcoursup

, the hated university admissions system, cap first-year high school classes at 28, and add 500 teaching posts. And in Serbia, a student movement that began after a railway station canopy 

collapsed in Novi Sad two years ago

 turned itself into an electoral list and, on Oct. 25, 

beat Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s strongman of 14 years

. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Facts like these are why, in my organizing circles, there’s a lot of talk of a “European wave.” I think we should be careful with that phrase, though, because it suggests a level of coordination and a plan that doesn’t — yet — exist. The reporting I trust describes these protests as 

“largely unconnected”

: common causes, solidarity marches and viral calls, but no shared target, no joint demands, and nobody deciding anything together across borders.




The closest thing to coordination is an 

international student strike

 on Nov. 20, which I’ll come back to. Because I think it shows both what this moment could become, and what it’s missing.




Why “no” is cheap




So why, with so much energy on the streets sustained over two months, has so little been won? Serbia is the exception, because its movement is two years old and has organized itself, faculty by faculty, from the start. Elsewhere, I think it comes down to two things—one that is out of protesters’ hands, and one that isn’t entirely. 







A government can wait out a crowd that hasn’t said what it wants, from whom and by when, or what it will take away if it doesn’t get it.







First, European governments have learned how to absorb a crowd. There’s no evidence they’re coordinating, but they have landed on remarkably similar responses. Italy sent 

500 troops to Milan after riots in October

 and passed an emergency decree that makes it easier to hold youth 14 and older criminally responsible. France 

deployed soldiers to guard public buildings

, 

banned protests in several cities

 and imposed a curfew in parts of Paris. By Oct. 8, French police had taken 

6,877 people into custody

, about 80 percent of them children. Portuguese police 

cleared the housing camps

 in Lisbon and Porto before dawn.







And most governments have found a way to say no to protesters’ demands: France 

opened a “consultation”

 and made 

partial offers

, Portugal said it “will not give in to 

shouts from the street,

” and Greece 

pointed to money

 it says it’s already spending.




Behind all this is the fact that time is on the government’s side in most of these countries. As Arundhati Roy 

put it

 in a recent essay about India’s Cockroach movement, states have the power to wait, but people don’t. Erica Chenoweth’s research found that even as nonviolent campaigns became more popular through the 2010s, their 

success rate fell

, partly because states got smarter, and partly because movements leaned on mobilizing people rather than organizing them. 




The second thing is that a government can wait out a crowd that hasn’t said what it wants, from whom and by when, or what it will take away if it doesn’t get it. And from observing what most of these protests do in public, that’s where they are. Their demands keep getting lost, and few of their actions seem aimed at the person who can say yes, or timed to a moment when that person needs something. (Spain and Belgium are the exceptions, and I’ll come back to both.)




And when a movement doesn’t define itself, everybody else gets to define it for them. The mainstream press focused mostly on the violence, and even sympathetic commentators turned the protests into a 

test of the EU’s survival

. Donald Trump announced that 

“the migrants have taken over France.”

 An 

AI-generated photo

 of an elderly couple supposedly stripped by rioters got 

a million views

 and was 

shared by a French police union

. Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, blamed “

foreign hands

” and said the protests were “not a student phenomenon.” And parts of the left, my own corner included, did the same thing from the other direction, arguing that a crowd that had come out over missing teachers was actually protesting about Gaza, or arms dealers, or capitalism.




That fight decides who turns up at the next protest and, critically, who gets to position themselves as the answer. In France, Marine Le Pen gave a 

solemn address in front of a French flag

 after the Oct. 17 riots, and the first poll afterwards put her at 

36 percent, up from 32 in September

. If the students don’t define their movement, the candidate of “order” will.




Four old questions




When faced with an organizing problem, I go back to the oldest questions in campaigning: Who can give you what you want — in other words, who decides? What exactly are you asking them to do? By when? And what leverage can’t they ignore?




1. Who decides?




The default answer to “who decides” is almost always “the government.” That isn’t wrong, but it’s too vague to be useful, because a government is hundreds of people with different jobs. And the decision-maker who can say yes to a particular demand may not be the one people are marching against. Take two of the French students’ demands: smaller classes and more teachers. Class sizes, it turns out, the government could change itself, and it 

offered a cap within weeks

. But teaching posts are in the budget, which is up to parliament, and the next vote is in the 

Senate on Dec. 9.

 Two demands, two different targets.




Students in Belgium worked this out early. The tuition increase at French-speaking universities wasn’t set by the federal government, but by 

the parliament of the French-speaking community

. So that’s where they took the fight: they 

protested

 before the decree passed in June, and now they’re 

taking it to the Constitutional Court, which can overturn unconstitutional laws.

 They haven’t won yet — but they are fighting in the right venue.




Working out exactly who decides takes more work than it sounds. But the point is: It’s usually done by a few people around a laptop on a Monday night, rather than in the streets on a Saturday. 




2. What are you asking?




When I went hunting for what the French students were actually asking for, I had to find their national coordination’s communiqué on 

an activist website

 because almost no English-language outlet had reported it. It mixed things a minister could grant tomorrow, like scrapping Parcoursup, with things no one could grant at all, like an end to inequality between rich and poor neighborhoods. When I 

posted about this

, several people messaged me to say these weren’t even the demands most of the movement backed. 




Movements with clear demands mostly arrive at them the same way: They put them to a vote among the people doing the marching, or at least consult them. Serbia’s students decided theirs in 

open assemblies at every faculty

, by show of hands.  In Spain, the Tenants’ Union didn’t pick the date for its general strike on its own; it 

talked to the protesters first

, then brought it to the big unions. A list people have voted for is much harder for anyone else to rewrite. 




Previous Coverage

 

How Serbian students toppled an authoritarian




And a list that is short, fixed and public is much harder for governments to dodge. Serbia’s protesters held to 

four demands

 for months — so when the government claimed it had met them all, they could rebut it point by point. But France’s “yellow vest” movement in 2018 had 

42 demands

, which let Emmanuel Macron pick the ones he liked — and launch a national debate that split the movement. 




Last, the demands that stick are usually the most concrete ones. “Maximum class sizes of 25” is something you can measure and chase; an end to inequality is a vision nobody can grant, so a government can wait it out forever. I’ve 

made this argument before:

 Keep the end goal, but give people a fight they can win on the way. Or, as 

Mark and Paul Engler put it

, make demands that are “both practical and visionary.” 




3. By when?




Then there’s the date. On Oct. 18, the first weekend of the school holidays, France’s student coordination 

set its next national day of protest

 for Nov. 3, just after the holidays end. This was a smart move, because people who go away need to know when to come back. The harder part, though, is pointing that protest date at a decision:  a vote, a deadline, a meeting where someone has to say yes or no. Belgium’s students did that with the June vote; Spain’s tenants, below, did it with an election.




4. What can’t they ignore?




This is the pressure point. I don’t mean public pressure, which is a tactic; I mean something your target 

needs

, from someone specific, at a particular moment. Whose vote do they depend on? Who are 

they

 asking for something? The date tells you when they decide; the pressure point is what would make them decide your way.




Spain offers the clearest example of getting this right. The Tenants’ Union, which has spent nearly a decade building rent strikes, 

picked Nov. 11

 for the general strike, 18 days before Spain’s snap election. Pedro Sánchez’s Socialists are 

trailing in the polls

, and what they need is for voters who care about rent to turn out for them. By putting housing at the center of the campaign, the strike makes every party compete for those votes.




The union has also refused to let any party 

identify with the strike or frame it

 as an attack on rival parties. It isn’t against “the other side,” said its spokesperson, but against “the rentier system.” That makes it much harder for anyone to relabel.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













And a strike asks just a day’s pay of the people taking part while costing the economy dearly — by one bank’s estimate, 

up to 0.2 percent of annual GDP

. “We, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora of the Madrid Tenants’ Union 

told Spanish radio

. Organizers say about four million people took part.




Of course, none of this guarantees a good result on Nov. 29, and the right may still win. But the point is: Spain is what a protest looks like when it’s attached to something a government can’t wait out.




And when there’s no pressure point to find, some movements build one. Serbia’s students spent two years marching for demands that were never fully met. In the end they stopped asking Vučić for anything and simply built the thing that could take power from him: 

a list of candidates

 with no party, no leader and one material grievance — corruption. That took two years, not two months.




From a date to a target




Which brings me back to Nov. 20. For the first time, if it all goes to plan, students in a dozen or so countries will walk out on the same day. The walkout was called by a small network of 

student and left-wing groups

, months before the French protests began. But this autumn’s movements have since picked it up: Italy’s national student organizations have 

adopted it

, Italy’s biggest union has 

called a general strike

 for the same day, and in Berlin, high school students will be 

marching with teachers’ unions

.




The youth strike’s first demand

 is the one that runs through almost every protest this autumn: “Investments in welfare, public education, healthcare and youth instead of weapons and militaries.” That’s an answer to the “what.” But it doesn’t yet have a “who” or a “when.”. Money for weapons and schools is decided in budgets, by parliaments, on dates set well in advance. And a budget vote is a moment when a government needs something it may not have: the votes in parliament. Whose votes are in doubt, and what would make them think twice, is the last question. And it’s what turns a date into a target.




Those riot police in Syntagma could afford to look bored, because they knew the march would be over by evening. A crowd on its own can be waited out. A crowd that keeps coming back — to the right decision-makers, at the right moment, and able to take away something they need — is much harder to ignore. 




The march shows how many people care. But the campaign is what you do with them.

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?

title: How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline
content:
This article 

How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On Nov. 7, the eve of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, the leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, including founder Abhijeet Dipke, were not at home. They were marching in Kochi, a port city in the southern state of Kerala, nearly 1,300 miles from Delhi. 




The march echoed the two demands the movement had been shouting in Delhi’s streets since the first week of October: Scrap the nationwide recheck of voter rolls that began in June 2025, and sack the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. 




The Cockroach movement came into being in May of this year and won its first victory in July, pushing India’s education minister out of office over a leaked national medical entrance exam. The open question then was whether 

a movement with no one leader and no office

 would still be around after winning its first fight. It is, and while it still has no office, it has picked a much bigger fight. Not an exam this time, but the vote itself.




The Election Commission, which runs India’s elections, is rechecking every one of India’s nearly one billion voters. In the name of clearing the rolls of the dead, the duplicated, people who have moved and what its 

June 2025 order

 called “foreign illegal immigrants,” it has 

purged more than 130 million

 voters. In Delhi alone, the cleanup has knocked 4.76 million people, nearly a third of the city’s electorate, off the voter list. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, strongly backs the recheck, saying that it’s necessary to strike undocumented migrants from neighboring Bangladesh, particularly Muslims, who have slipped onto the rolls. Amit Shah, Modi’s home minister and most powerful lieutenant, has defended the recheck as a way to “detect, delete, deport” what he calls infiltrators. 

But critics charge

 that the rolls are being manipulated to benefit the BJP. They say the recheck shifts the burden of proof onto voters, and that the people least likely to have the required documents are the ones being dropped. 




Human Rights Watch found

 that the purge has disproportionately affected women, the poor and Muslims; in one area of West Bengal that is nine percent Muslim, more than 92 percent of those deleted were Muslim. 

Opposition leaders

 have called the recheck a backdoor version of the National Register of Citizens, a citizenship list the BJP promised in 2019 to extend across India.




Presiding over it all is Kumar, whose commission both referees India’s elections and runs the recheck. He was handpicked by Modi in February 2025 under a new law giving Modi more power over the selection, in a decision announced late at night over the written dissent of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.




In late September, the national daily 

The Indian Express

 

reported

 that two of the election commission’s three members, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders tied to the recheck that they say were issued in the commission’s name without their knowledge. (In an official statement, the commission maintained that all of its decisions on the recheck were unanimous.) 




Previous Coverage

 

What India’s Cockroach Party won — and what’s next




The Cockroach movement, which had been pressuring the government since July over broken promises, responded by calling Kumar the biggest threat to India’s democracy and giving him 48 hours to resign.




When Kumar ignored the movement’s deadline, it took to the streets of Delhi and other cities on Oct. 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India’s nonviolent struggle for independence.




Unlike most Indian police forces, Delhi’s police do not answer to the city’s elected government but to the federal Home Ministry, run by Shah. It answered the protests the way it did in July, only harder. On Oct. 10 police detained more than 2,000 people in Delhi, opposition leaders and journalists among them, while about 600 were detained in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and mobile internet went dark in the heart of Delhi.




Two days later

, Jantar Mantar — a square just a short walk from Parliament that has been Delhi’s main protest site for decades and was occupied by the movement for five weeks this summer — was struck off the list of places where protest is allowed. Two of the movement’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, walked into Jantar Mantar with the national flag the next day and were arrested. They were jailed for a week for breaking a peace bond and still face criminal charges. 




Through all of this, the protests have stayed nonviolent and they have spread well beyond Delhi. In Kochi, hundreds of people marched behind the actor and activist Prakash Raj under the banner “Jantar Mantar @ Kochi.”




I spoke with Ratna Singh, who leads the CJP’s legal team, over a series of WhatsApp voice calls in early November, about how the movement holds its nonviolent line under this much pressure, and what comes next.




Ratna Singh (left) and Saurav Das (right) exit court proceedings on Aug. 18, 2026 in Delhi. (Ishant Chauhan/Hindustan Times via Getty Images)




This interview was conducted in Hindi and has been translated and edited for length and clarity.




Your movement started over an exam. Now it’s about the vote. Who are you really fighting, the Election Commission or Modi?




It’s the same fight. We can’t question how an election is run without questioning the government that runs it. Let’s stop pretending these are separate things.




The BJP’s attitude is, “You voted, now shut up and obey.” That’s democratic tyranny. Citizens have every right to check the rolls, expose manipulation and ask for complete transparency.




What really gets me is how state media treats the BJP as if it were the nation. The government cannot claim to speak for the entire country. Modi is the prime minister, but Indian democracy belongs to its citizens.




People came out in October because they’d had enough of that arrogance. We’re not begging for crumbs. We want accountability, and we’ll take it.




The crackdown came fast. How do you get people ready for that, and keep them nonviolent when the police move in?




We brief everyone before every march: no panic, no retaliation. When police charge or bring out detention buses, our instruction is to sit down on the pavement immediately. Sitting down takes away their excuse to claim we were rushing them or inciting a riot.




It forces the police to physically carry people away one by one, which slows them down and exposes their aggression on camera. Nonviolence here isn’t passive; it’s an active tactic to strip the state of its excuses.




The state’s favorite trick is to change the story. People are out there over stolen elections, and suddenly the debate is about unlawful assembly and traffic permits. That’s deliberate. It keeps the government away from real scrutiny.




I tell people to remain disciplined and understand their legal rights. That does not mean they should stop questioning the authorities. We can remain peaceful while continuing to challenge the government.




There’s no single leader. So, who keeps the discipline?




Indian politics is sick with hero worship, and the BJP is the worst case. Everything revolves around the cult of Modi: the propaganda, the policy, the state machinery. That’s not strength. That’s a single point of failure. We’re not going to build another political god. 




A real movement runs on shared anger and a clear strategy, not on waiting for one boss to give orders. The movement depends on people understanding its objectives and taking responsibility for their actions. We don’t need one person making every decision.




In large, leaderless crowds, how do you stop someone from throwing stones or provoking violence?




The state’s oldest trick is sending in provocateurs to throw a stone, turn a march violent and justify a crackdown. We deploy trained marshals and experienced volunteers across the crowd. The moment someone starts acting aggressively or picks up a projectile, our volunteers immediately surround that person, isolate them and calm the crowd down. We make it clear: Anyone inciting violence is working for the regime, not the movement.




Mobile internet was shut down in central Delhi during the protests. How do you coordinate when you’re offline?




You can’t rely solely on WhatsApp or social media when you’re fighting a state that controls the kill switch. We operate on a decentralized structure. We use pre-agreed physical contact points, runner systems and offline mesh networks to pass instructions.




Small local teams know their primary and secondary assembly spots in advance. If the internet goes dark, the plan doesn’t change. Everyone knows where to be and what their role is.




Critics say you’re being provocative on purpose. Are you?




Absolutely. That’s the whole point of resistance. If you’re not threatening the status quo, you’re just putting on a show for the regime.




“Provocative” is what people in power call you when they’re losing their grip on citizens. They want polite dissent with no teeth, petitions they can drop straight in the bin.




But there’s a huge line between physical violence and hard political confrontation. And the BJP built its empire on ruthless political violence. It has no right to lecture its victims about manners. If asking questions provokes them, it just shows how long they’ve been coddled.




The government says the mass detentions were just routine law and order.




That’s a pathetic, cowardly excuse. The minute the state’s legitimacy is questioned, it hides behind police batons and calls it public safety.




Look at the double standard. The BJP can shut down whole cities for its own rallies, and that’s national pride. Ordinary citizens gather to question the government, and suddenly they’re a national security threat.




If our accusations are false, why hide the data and the sources? If the system isn’t rigged, prove it. Sending in police boots to crush dissent isn’t governance. It’s state terror. And attacking Modi is a democratic duty, not treason.




Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Tihar jail over a peace bond, and they’re still facing charges. What’s the point of all this legal pressure?




It’s judicial harassment. The repeated summonses and legal cases put enormous pressure on activists and their families. Even when a protest is peaceful, people have to spend time and money dealing with these cases. We believe the legal process is being used to discourage people from continuing the movement.




How does your legal team handle thousands of detentions in a single day?




It’s a war of attrition. We have a network of volunteer lawyers stationed across different police stations and magistrate courts in the city. As soon as a detention bus leaves, our ground volunteers send the vehicle number and station location through our backup channels.




Lawyers arrive before the buses to monitor treatment, track names and draft bail bonds on the spot. They want to wear us down with paperwork and legal costs, but our legal network works 24/7 to make sure no activist is left behind.




Jantar Mantar is now closed to protest. What does that say about Modi’s government?




This blows apart Modi’s whole international act. He travels the world selling India as the “Mother of Democracy,” and at home he runs a police state that chokes basic speech.




Jantar Mantar was set aside for people to protest, not for parades the state approves of. When they use red tape to outlaw political opposition, that’s not regulation. That’s totalitarian control.




If the state only allows protests that pose no risk to it, democracy is already dead. What’s left is a show.




What has kept people coming back for four months, with all this pressure?




The core crime hasn’t gone away.




The BJP survives on short attention spans. Every 72 hours there’s a new crisis or another distraction pitting Hindus against Muslims to flood the news, and then they wait for people to forget.




But electoral fraud and captured institutions don’t disappear just because the TV channels move on. 




Women have been at the front of these protests. What does that change?




It wrecks the BJP’s gender washing. They use women as props in their campaign ads. Real empowerment is women on the street standing up to state power.




When a woman stands up and calls out Modi’s regime, that’s direct political action. You can’t praise women as obedient voters in your speeches and then send riot police after them the moment they turn against you.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













What did the recent gathering in Kochi show you?




It kills the regime’s line that this is a tantrum by Delhi elites.




Electoral corruption is a national disease. The BJP badly wants every protest to look local, because a united, nationwide resistance threatens its grip on power.




Kochi shows it’s crossing state lines. Modi’s government can’t contain this as a local disturbance anymore. The anger is spreading, and the state can’t arrest an entire country.




People have until Nov. 25 to file objections and corrections to the recheck, and the final list comes out on Dec. 22. If millions are still missing, is that the end of it?




Right now, it’s maximum pressure through Nov. 25 and Dec. 22. We won’t let the state use those dates as a blanket to smother the questions about the rolls.




Will the CJP run for office in the 2027 state elections or the 2029 general election?




It’s a real strategic option. But turning into just another party is a trap. If we end up copying the BJP’s centralization, its high handedness, its autocratic habits, then the whole struggle has failed.




The Modi regime isn’t invincible. Its dominance is an illusion kept alive by fear. But empty slogans against Modi won’t do it. You need an aggressive alternative that takes apart the power structure.




The people are sovereign, not Narendra Modi. The BJP has no divine right to rule. If we get on the ballot, it’ll be to smash this culture of unchecked power, not to swap one dictator for another. We’re not here to cause a temporary disturbance. We’re here to bring the political establishment to its knees.

author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article 

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.




Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party, 

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was 

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.




The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won 

more seats in Congress than any other

 

—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties, 

gave the right a majority in both houses

.




Two days after the vote, 

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he 

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.




“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”





In addition, whoever won in October would be able to 

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

, 

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.




As a result, after the first-round results came in on 

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.




Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one 

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.




Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.




For Gabriel Rochlin, 

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”




From demoralization to esperançar




Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










“When we got hit with the news that Flávio had more votes, there was a kind of desperation,” said Nayara Ruiz, a social media strategist with 

280,000 followers on Instagram

. “A huge shock, a feeling of fear, and a replay in our heads of 

2018 [when Jair Bolsonaro was elected].” At first, Ruiz recorded a video about that fear. “And while I was editing it, I started to feel really bad. And I said: I’m not going to post this video, this is not the path I need to take.” She came across a news story about how online fandoms dedicated to Brazilian and international musical artists like 

Taylor Swift, BTS and Anitta were putting their networks at the service of Lula’s campaign. “The moment I saw that, I said: ‘That’s it, I have to talk about this, about esperançar.’”




“Esperançar,” was a term used by Brazilian educator Paulo Freire to mean “hope in action,” as opposed to “esperar,” which in Portuguese means both to hope and to wait.




Ruiz then recorded 

a video

 talking about the fandoms and about esperançar, and why it matters for organizing. She explained that esperançar demands three things: seeing a possible future, understanding that there is a path to that future, and feeling that you can do something to make that path a reality. She wanted to show that there was a path to defeat Flávio if people came together.




The video was 

viewed 5 million times, the most of any she had posted, and brought her 40,000 new followers, Ruiz said. It was one of many videos and posts in the days after the first-round vote that spoke to people’s discouragement and helped turn it into a willingness to act.




Social media activism may have been one of the left’s most innovative strategies in this campaign. A WhatsApp channel called Exército do Lula, or Lula’s Army, was created by André Janones, a federal congressman from the state of Minas Gerais. What set it apart was its scale and its structure. It quickly grew from 

50,000

 

to 

more than 10 million followers

 in less than three weeks, in a country where WhatsApp had been the far right’s most effective tool since Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018 campaign.




“We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




The channel’s growth came as the Lula campaign charged that Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, had limited the reach of Lula’s posts and favored Flávio’s. (

Leaked communications from inside Meta

 supported this, and Meta acknowledged “technical problems” with the Lula campaign’s paid promotions, but denied any bias.) For Lula’s Army, the WhatsApp channel had the advantage of delivering messages directly to its followers without an algorithm throttling their reach.




Rather than relying on a few official accounts to broadcast the Lula campaign’s message, it turned millions of ordinary supporters into active participants. It also gamified the organizing for the second round. Because voting is compulsory in Brazil, the goal was less to get out the vote than to reduce abstention and win over undecided voters. Through frequent audio messages, videos and texts, Janones handed out missions to participants, calling on them to share content, boost posts, promote hashtags, invite new members and amplify messages supporting the campaign. Everyone was given a rank and could advance up the ladder by completing these tasks. Janones “promoted” Ruiz from soldier to captain of the Army in a 

lighthearted video

 because of the explainer videos she made about the channel.




She believes one of the initiative’s contributions was fostering a kind of political digital literacy among supporters. Janones taught the channel’s followers how platform algorithms work, so that messages from Lula and critical information about Flávio would rank higher on social media. Until then, the far right had dominated social media, partly because of the high engagement its posts generated. Participants in Lula’s Army came to understand that part of that engagement came precisely from their reacting to far-right content that bothered them.




Previous Coverage

 

How a strong messaging strategy helped defeat Brazil’s Bolsonaro




Janones’ strategic directive to Lula’s supporters was that they should stop interacting with opponents’ posts and concentrate their collective strength on producing and circulating their own content. To that end, participants were instructed to watch videos to the end, and to like, comment on, save and share posts, using the platforms’ different features to expand their reach.




“Maybe Lula wouldn’t have won without this, without the Army, without this feeling that swept over people, without the sense that we weren’t fighting alone,” Ruiz said. “We learned together, we mobilized together, we practiced esperançar together, we believed together, and Lula’s Army was a place that brought all of that together.”




Ruiz credits Janones with turning that collective energy into a coordinated effort. “Janones calls himself a general, but I also see him very much as a conductor who led an orchestra that was disorganized, who tuned the instruments and managed to set the rhythm and organize the whole mobilization that took place and that is now being replicated around the world,” Ruiz said.




Taking to the streets




Social media also played an important role in spreading the word about and organizing the occupation of the streets during the weeks before the runoff. In the three weeks between Oct. 4 and Oct. 25, 

massive peaceful protests

 brought together hundreds of thousands of demonstrators across the country. 

These 

protests featured politicians, renowned Brazilian musicians

 like Chico Buarque, Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil, and grassroots artistic groups. Together, the iconic faces and grassroots artists helped bring in a very broad diversity of people.




“As we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”





University students played a fundamental role in this occupation of the streets. They were the ones who kicked things off on Oct. 5, and throughout the three weeks between the first and second round of voting, they were a major force calling people to the protests, often organizing through their own social media.




The 

first street protest of the runoff campaign took place in Niterói

 in the state of Rio de Janeiro on Oct. 5, organized by students from Fluminense Federal University. Those students set an example, according to Gabriel Shpielman, a mathematics student and activist with the Rebellious Youth Union. “I think if that hadn’t happened on the first day, it would have been totally different,” he said.




Student mobilization quickly spread to other universities, including the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, or PUC-Rio, which also began organizing the day after the first round. Shpielman and a classmate created an Instagram profile and called on students at the university to attend an assembly, from which the 

PUC-Rio Antifascista

 movement was born. Around 200 students packed the auditorium, heard from a representative of the National Union of Students 

a

nd decided to go together to the protest in downtown Rio the following day.




According to Shpielman, this helped “put people in the position of seeing themselves building the comeback.” For him, it was in this experience with their collective strength that fear gave way to organizing: “At first it reflected despair, but as we saw the big street protests, the power we had, not only inside the university but also in the streets, on social media too, it started creating a movement of hope.”




The call for student protest started by word of mouth, in classrooms and WhatsApp groups, and gained reach through PUC-Rio Antifascista’s Instagram account. The account shared collaborative posts — Instagram posts that appear on several accounts at once — with other accounts, like 

Protesto Estudantil

 (a page run by high school students from Colégio Pedro II), 

the PUC-Rio Graduate Students’ Association, and with public figures such as Dani Balbi, Anielle Franco, Wagner Moura and Chico Buarque.




Students march in a rally for Lula at PUC-Rio on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Tatiana Chain)




Shpielman called the process cyclical: The more visibility PUC-Rio Antifascista gained, the more partnerships it secured, and those partnerships increased its visibility. The page has now reached over 30,000 followers. Even so, for him, social media was at the service of the streets. “What really turned the election around were the streets, the protests,” he said. “Social media reflected that mobilization. It’s so much better to see a protest with a million people than a page with 10 million people.”




Getting voters to the polls




Another point of concern in the first round was the abstention rate, which was the highest since 1998: Over 

21 percent

 of eligible voters, or 33.4 million people, simply didn’t vote. In light of this, much of civil society’s mobilization sought to make sure people went to vote. This took place through 

crowdfunding drives

 to arrange transportation for those living far from their polling places, ride-sharing initiatives, providing information for undecided voters in the streets and vira voto campaigns.




Diego Zuculin is one of the founders of 

Casa Marighella

, a cultural and artistic production company and organization in São Paulo that put all of its work on hold to get out the vote. After the first-round results, “everyone looked at each other and said: ‘Wow, we’re screwed. What are we going to do?’,” Zuculin said. The next morning, the team decided “almost everything could be postponed in the face of the end of democracy.”




The first idea was simple: He would offer his own car to neighbors whose grandparents had no way to get to the polls, and a friend would offer his motorcycle. They soon realized that many people were probably thinking the same thing and decided to create a platform connecting those who could offer rides on election day with those who needed them. That’s how 

Carona Solidária

, or Solidarity Ride, was born.




The team developed the first version of the platform in-house in two or three days. As word spread, partner collectives, artists, tech people and lawyers joined to help with legal issues and with outreach. The platform circulated on Instagram and WhatsApp, and in a second phase, the group reached out to journalists and pages in Brazil’s North region, where there were still few ride offers.




“The heart of vira voto is its humanity. It’s a place for building bonds, for looking people in the eye.”




“We had an idea, we put it to work, then it went to social media and it spread across all of Brazil,” Zuculin said. 

A total of 22,000 rides were offered, in every state and the Federal District, and the real reach was even greater. “Some people told us: ‘I registered two people, but I took two, and on the way back I took three more, and then five more.’ One person posted a video saying they drove 13 people, another 15, and only registered one or two.”




He also says that the reasons users gave when requesting a ride — such as a distant polling place, no nearby buses, advanced age or having to work on election day — could serve as a basis for public policy. In the second round, abstention fell to 

19.22 percent

, the lowest for a runoff since 2006, the result of an effort of which, Zuculin acknowledges, Carona Solidária was only one part.




Complementing these efforts, numerous vira voto campaigns took place across the country, in which people organized in groups to go out on the streets and talk to voters, especially those who were undecided or planning to abstain. Lula himself issued this call 

in a video posted on Oct. 7

: “Come on, everyone, to the streets, let’s talk to people.” 




In Rio de Janeiro, the local WhatsApp group that Gabriel Rochlin belonged to started with fewer than 10 people and ended with 60. Over two and a half weeks, according to the group’s own count, they flipped 181 votes. “Thinking of vira voto as collective action gives you a much greater sense of accomplishment,” he said. The group set up at Largo do Machado square and in front of the Catete Palace because, according to Rochlin, Workers’ Party congressman-elect Marcelo Freixo had indicated that there were many undecided voters there. WhatsApp was used to organize the actions and to make sure volunteers were always together and in safe places, given the risk of violence.
